title: Green chemistry and nanotechnology
summary: Learn to prevent waste from the start, get to know the nanoscale, and look at plastics and energy through a green lens.
cards.0.p: Green chemistry means designing products and processes to be harmless from the start. The first of its 12 principles is: preventing waste is better than cleaning it up after it forms.
cards.0.svg#8: First of 12 principles: prevent waste from the start
cards.0.key: Using less and safer material, less energy, renewable feedstocks and products that break down in nature are also among the principles. The cleanest waste is the waste that never forms.
cards.0.once.soru: Which is the greener solution for a factory?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Waste that never forms needs no treatment, energy or risk.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Treatment is good, but it uses energy. Preventing waste from the start is better.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Moving waste does not get rid of it. It only changes its location.
cards.1.p: You can run the same reaction with a few drops in a well plate instead of a beaker. You see the same thing, but chemicals, rinse water and waste drop by dozens of times.
cards.1.svg#2: Same reaction, far less chemical and waste
cards.1.key: The experiment becomes fast, safe and cheap. Microscale work is the easiest way to apply green chemistry in a school lab.
cards.2.p: 1 nm is one billionth of a meter. A strand of hair is about 80000 nm thick. Particles 1-100 nm in size are called nanoparticles. At this size, the surface grows and the properties of matter change.
cards.2.svg#12: Each tick is bigger than the last (scale not even)
cards.2.key: Gold nanoparticles are red, not yellow. The substance is the same, but the size differs. So color and reaction rate can change.
cards.3.p: Used tea leaf extract contains polyphenols. These reduce the Ag⁺ ions in silver nitrate to Ag atoms. The atoms gather as nanoparticles, and the solution turns yellow-brown.
cards.3.key: The extract coats the particles and keeps them from clumping. Pomegranate peel works too. Copper nanoparticles are made in a similar way.
cards.4.p: In the comparison, only the type of waste changes. Amount, temperature and time are kept constant. If the peak is near 420 nm and has a similar shape, the sample with the larger blank-corrected absorbance has made more nanoparticles.
cards.4.svg#5: sample data: same time, temperature and amount
cards.4.key: The independent variable is the waste type, and the dependent variable is absorbance. The blank contains only the extract, so the extract's own color is subtracted. If the peak shifts, the particle size is different, and amounts cannot be compared directly.
cards.4.once.soru: You are comparing used tea leaf extract with pomegranate peel extract. What may you change?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: A fair test has a single variable, and everything else is kept constant.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: If two things change at once, you can't tell what caused the difference.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: If everything changes, the results cannot be compared.
cards.5.p: Heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium do not break down. Living things get rid of them slowly, so these metals build up in the body. Mercury becomes more concentrated as it moves up the food chain. This is called biomagnification.
cards.5.svg#4: Mercury leaves the body slowly, so its concentration rises at each level
cards.5.key: Bioaccumulation happens in a single organism, and biomagnification is seen along the food chain. In the 1950s in Minamata, mercury waste built up in fish and thousands of people were poisoned. Putting used batteries in a collection bin catches the metal before it enters the chain.
cards.6.p: Silver nanoparticles kill germs, so they are added to socks. Washing releases them into water, and treatment plants cannot catch them all. In nature, they can also harm useful bacteria.
cards.6.svg#6: solution: avoid needless use, design for safety
cards.6.key: Nanoscale size makes particles hard to separate from water. The solution is to cut needless use and design products to be safe from the start.
cards.6.once.soru: When socks with silver nanoparticles are washed, where does some of the silver go?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: With every wash, some of the particles get into the water.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The particles don't hold tightly to the fibers and decrease with each wash.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Silver does not evaporate. Water carries it away.
cards.7.p: Nano zinc oxide in sunscreen blocks UV rays without leaving a white film. Lipid nanoparticles carry mRNA vaccines. But breathable dusts and long-term effects are still a concern.
cards.7.svg#10: look at the evidence and the intended use
cards.7.key: Nano-coated glass cleans itself. The word "nano" on a product does not make it good or bad. What matters is the evidence and the purpose.
cards.7.once.soru: A product says "nano" on it. Does that show the product is safe?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: "Nano" only describes the size. Research shows whether it is safe.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Nanoscale size sometimes brings new risks too.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Being nano does not mean being natural or safe.
cards.8.p: Plastic smaller than 5 mm is called microplastic, and plastic smaller than 1 µm is called nanoplastic. The main sources are washing synthetic clothes and tire wear. Microplastics have even been found in human blood.
cards.8.svg#5: Plastic doesn't disappear, it breaks into smaller pieces
cards.8.key: Breaking-down packaging is also a source, and the health effects are being studied. Plastic does not disappear, it just gets smaller. The smaller it gets, the more easily it enters living things.
cards.8.once.soru: What happens to a plastic bottle in the sea over time?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Sunlight and waves break plastic apart. The pieces get smaller but do not disappear.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Plastic stays in nature for hundreds of years.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Plastic does not dissolve in water.
cards.9.p: PLA is made from corn starch. Starch becomes sugar, fermentation turns the sugar into lactic acid, and the lactic acid polymerizes. At home, you can also make a film from starch, water, vinegar and glycerol.
cards.9.svg#6: at home: starch + water + vinegar + glycerol
cards.9.key: Glycerol slips between the chains and makes the film flexible. Some bacteria store PHA. PLA usually breaks down quickly only in industrial compost.
cards.10.p: Some bacteria break down sugary waste without oxygen and release hydrogen. This is called dark fermentation. One glucose gives at most 4 H₂. When hydrogen burns, only water forms.
cards.10.svg#5: factors: waste type, pH, temperature, time
cards.10.key: The reaction is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 2H₂O → 2CH₃COOH + 2CO₂ + 4H₂. The yield depends on the waste type, pH, temperature and time.
cards.11.p: In a dye-sensitized solar cell, light is absorbed not by silicon but by a dye attached to TiO₂ nanoparticles. This cell is cheap, colorful and semitransparent. But its efficiency is lower than a silicon cell's.
cards.11.svg#7: cheap, colorful, good in dim light
cards.11.svg#8: The dye absorbs light, and an electron passes to TiO₂
cards.11.key: Efficiency is found by dividing the electrical power by the incoming light power and multiplying by 100. The best cells reach 13-15%. This cell works well in dim light, but it has a short lifetime.
cards.11.etk.soru: 100 mW of light falls on a 1 cm² cell. Change the current and voltage the cell gives. What is the efficiency?
cards.11.once.soru: 100 mW of light falls on a cell, and the cell gives 10 mW of electricity. What is the efficiency in percent?
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: 90% is the part that does not become electricity.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Efficiency is the electrical power divided by the light power, multiplied by 100.
cards.12.p: AI data centers use a lot of electricity and cooling water. But AI can quickly screen new battery and catalyst materials and manage the power grid efficiently.
cards.12.key: The impact depends on which energy it runs on and what it is used for. The question to ask is: are the savings bigger than the energy used?
cards.12.once.soru: How can you tell whether an AI project is good for the environment?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: If it saves more energy than it uses, it helps.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Running fast does not show any benefit to the environment.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Being new does not mean being eco-friendly.
cards.13.p:
• Green chemistry prevents waste from the start. Microscale work is an easy way to do this.
• Nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in size and can be made with waste extracts.
• Heavy metals and nanoparticles can build up in nature.
• Microplastics get smaller but do not disappear.
• PLA, hydrogen from waste and dye solar cells are green options.
quiz.0.q: Sort each practice by whether it fits green chemistry.
quiz.0.ogeler.4.0: Throwing used batteries in the trash
quiz.0.e: Green chemistry prevents waste from the start and chooses renewable, safe materials. A needlessly large experiment creates waste. Used batteries release heavy metals. Microbeads get into water as microplastics.
quiz.1.q: Match the terms with their definitions.
quiz.1.e: The nanoscale is 1-100 nm. Microplastics are under 5 mm. A metal that living things cannot get rid of builds up step by step along the food chain. Polyphenols in the extract reduce silver ions to metal.
quiz.2.q: Put the steps of making PLA in order (first at the top).
quiz.2.e: Starch breaks down into sugar, bacteria turn the sugar into lactic acid, and lactic acid molecules link together to form the PLA chain.
quiz.3.q: You are studying how the type of household waste affects hydrogen production by fermentation. Which of these is a control variable that must be kept constant?
quiz.3.e: Waste type is the independent variable, and hydrogen volume is the dependent variable. Temperature, pH, amount of waste and time must be kept constant. Otherwise you can't know what caused the difference.
quiz.3.y.0: Waste type is the independent variable that you change.
quiz.3.y.1: Hydrogen volume is the result you measure, so it is the dependent variable.
quiz.3.y.3: If you change several things at once, you can't know what caused the difference.
A:ozet: Compare a macro and a micro experiment, cut a cube down to the nanoscale, make silver nanoparticles with waste extract, watch mercury build up along the food chain, tune a starch film and get hydrogen from waste.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Run the same reaction first in a beaker, then in a well plate. Compare the two with the switch.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: At microscale, by what factor did the waste drop?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Waste dropped from 50 mL to 0.5 mL, and 50 ÷ 0.5 = 100. Chemicals also dropped 100 times, and rinse water 25 times.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Work out 50 ÷ 0.5. The result is much larger than 10.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Look at the bars. The microscale waste is barely visible.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Cut a 1 cm³ cube into smaller and smaller cubes. Make the total surface area about 60 m², about the floor of a classroom.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: When the edge reaches 100 nm, the surface of 1 cm³ of material reaches 60 m². Reactions happen at surfaces, which is why nanoparticles are so reactive.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Each time the edge is divided by 10, the surface grows 10 times.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Extract made from used tea leaves will be dripped into silver nitrate solution.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What is seen in the solution?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Polyphenols in the extract reduce Ag⁺ ions to Ag. The silver nanoparticles that form absorb light and give the solution a yellow-brown color.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Blue is typical of copper(II) ions. Here there is silver.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The extract is a reducing agent. It reacts with Ag⁺, and the color changes.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You will make copper nanoparticles from pomegranate peel the same way as with silver. Set up the experiment plan.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: Polyphenols in pomegranate peel reduce Cu²⁺ ions to Cu atoms, and heat speeds up the reaction. Copper nanoparticles have an absorbance peak near 570 nm. Copper oxidizes easily in air, so the measurement is made right away.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: Adapt the steps of the silver experiment to copper.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Extracts from three wastes were mixed with silver nitrate using the same amount, temperature and time. Compare the results.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Which extract made the most silver nanoparticles?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The conditions are the same and the peaks are in the same place, so the sizes are similar. The largest blank-corrected absorbance means the most particles.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The absorbance of used tea leaves (0.62) is smaller than that of pomegranate peel (0.95).
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Orange peel has the smallest absorbance (0.31). It also has the fewest particles.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The same comparison was made with copper sulfate. One result is different from the others.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which result cannot be compared directly with the others?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: This sample's peak has shifted to 640 nm. So the particles have a different size or type (for example, oxidized copper). Its absorbance is large, but the amount cannot be compared directly.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: This sample's peak is in the copper range (about 570 nm). So it can be compared with the others.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: This sample's peak is in the copper range (about 570 nm). Its absorbance is small, but it can be compared.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A small amount of mercury waste got into a lake. Follow the food chain.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Where is the mercury concentration highest?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: At the top of the chain, in humans
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Each organism eats many prey and gets rid of mercury much more slowly than it takes it in. The concentration multiplies at each level. This is called biomagnification.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The concentration is lowest in the water. Mercury passes into living things and builds up there.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Mercury leaves the body slowly, so it concentrates at the upper levels.
A:adimlar.7.metin: You are making a film with 10 g of starch. Adjust the glycerol amount. The film should be flexible, neither brittle nor sticky.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.tamam: Glycerol slips between the starch chains and pushes them slightly apart. So the film bends but does not fall apart. Designing a polymer means choosing its ingredients for the purpose.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.ipucu: If the film cracks, add glycerol. If it is sticky, use less.
A:adimlar.8.metin: Set the pH and temperature, then press play. Collect the most hydrogen in the balloon.
A:adimlar.8.gorev.tamam: A slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.5) and warm (≈ 35 °C) environment suits these bacteria best. In a real experiment, the waste type, amount and time are kept constant.
A:adimlar.8.gorev.ipucu: Make the environment slightly acidic and bring the temperature close to body temperature.
A:kapanis.0: Preventing waste is better than cleaning it up. Microscale work makes this possible in the lab.
A:kapanis.1: As matter gets smaller, its surface grows. At the nanoscale, matter behaves differently.
A:kapanis.2: Silver and copper nanoparticles can be made with waste extracts. In the comparison, the only variable is the waste type. If the peak position is the same, blank-corrected absorbances are compared.
A:kapanis.3: Heavy metals build up in living things. Mercury becomes more concentrated step by step along the food chain.
A:kapanis.4: A biodegradable film and hydrogen from waste depend on choosing the ingredients and conditions.
